extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in undergraduate mathematics education (university instructors, mathematics education researchers, curriculum designers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical-evaluation standards for implementing and assessing a blended instructional method (Memphis Mathematics Method) using MyMathLab in undergraduate general-education mathematics courses, including study design, outcome definitions, and statistical modeling choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blended instructional method as ideal for learning
rubrics_metrics.description: This evidence suggests that a blended instructional method—technology coupled with guided lecture—may be ideal for increasing learning and success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification cites alignment with theoretical orientations (cognitive flexibility, embodied cognition, integrating abstract and concrete representations, inquiry and knowledge building). Use a blend of instructional methods rather than pure student-centered discovery (Mayer, 2004).

rubrics_metrics.name: MyMathLab learning aids (five features)
rubrics_metrics.description: MyMathLab offers student aid features that align with elements identified in the literature as fostering increased student learning and understanding. These five learning aids are: (1) step-by-step worked solution of a similar problem, (2) video example, (3) just-in-time, (4) view an example, and (5) ask my instructor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each aid maps to learning principles: (1) scaffolding via worked solutions promotes deep understanding (VanLehn, 2006); (2) video examples leverage multimedia advantages (Mayer, 2005); (3) electronic textbook provides just-in-time access and retrospective learning (Bransford & Schwartz, 1999); (4) guided example-problem pairs align with worked-example research (Sweller & Chandler, 1994); (5) conversational aid parallels intelligent tutoring dialogues (VanLehn et al., 2007). Use these features when selecting interactive content-delivery software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class structure for the Memphis Mathematics Method (MMM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors employing the MMM begin each class with a 25-minute lecture followed by a problem-solving session using MyMathLab. Each lecture contains a list of objectives, a few illustrative examples, and mathematical problems for discussion. Over a 15-week semester, students log 30 hours of class time practicing problems on MyMathLab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remaining class time dedicated to solving problems chosen as a combination of review questions and problems related to the lecture; instructor and an assistant are available to provide individual help and technical support. This structure is central to implementation fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading and assessment composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Final grades are computed as a weighted sum of all the points earned throughout the semester, including attendance, in-class lab assignments, tests, quizzes, and a final exam. Students complete proctored tests and the final exam online in the instructional lab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use automated grading within the learning environment where possible; include attendance and in-class performance to reflect daily engagement in blended model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definition of 'success' outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Define an indicator variable 'success' coded as 1 if a student obtains a grade of C or above and 0 if they obtained a grade of D or F, or withdrew from the course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combines pass rate and dropout effects; be explicit about grade thresholds when comparing across pedagogies to ensure consistent outcome measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definition of 'dropout' outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Define an indicator variable 'dropout' coded as 1 if a student dropped out of a course and 0 if a student completed the course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dropout as a separate dependent variable to isolate retention effects of pedagogy distinct from course performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent variables to include in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the student’s gender, the student’s racial/ethnic background (White, Black, Hispanic, and Other), the student’s prior mathematics knowledge as measured by their ACT math score, and an indicator variable 'redo' coded as 1 if a student has attempted the course before and 0 if this is their first attempt. Also include an indicator for whether a student was exposed to the MMM pedagogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These covariates control for observable heterogeneity; explicitly report descriptive statistics (means, SDs, Ns) for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling interactions to measure differential impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Include interaction terms between the MMM pedagogy and race/ethnicity (e.g., X3 * X2 * β3 in the logit specification) to estimate whether the pedagogy differentially affects outcomes for racial/ethnic groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interaction coefficients quantify heterogeneous treatment effects (e.g., MMM * Black). Present both odds ratios and illustrative predicted probabilities to communicate substantive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimation approach: logistic regression for binary outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: To model the success rate and the dropout rate for both DSPM and regular courses, fit logistic regressions for each of the three courses separately and estimate interactive models for remedial and non-remedial courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify logit(pi) = ln(pi/(1-pi)) = a + X1iβ1 + X2iβ2 + X3i*X2iβ3 + ui. Report robust standard errors and significance levels (e.g., *** p<0.01). Because marginal effects on probability depend on other variables, compute predicted probabilities for representative students to illustrate effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting logistic coefficients and reporting predicted probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreting coefficients within a logistic regression is difficult since while the marginal effect on the logit or odds ratio is constant, the marginal effect on the probability depends on the other variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute and report predicted probabilities for concrete student profiles (example given: male Black student with average ACT score) to make findings interpretable (e.g., 29.0% vs. 78.2% chance of succeeding under different pedagogies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Course and sample selection for evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Include multiple course contexts (College Algebra, Foundations of Mathematics, Elementary Calculus) and both remedial (DSPM) and regular sections across multiple semesters (fall 2007 to spring 2010) with transparent enrollment counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting enrollments by course and teaching method (traditional vs MMM) supports assessment of generalizability and subgroup analyses; ensure prerequisites and student eligibility criteria are documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proctored online exams for assessment integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Students complete proctored tests and the final exam online in the instructional lab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proctoring in lab reduces academic integrity concerns when assessments are administered online; record administration modality when comparing outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability and cost-effectiveness criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: From a practical standpoint, postsecondary institutions need to find a cost effective, scalable, and impactful method. After initial start-up cost, MMM allows employing undergraduate student assistants rather than graduate students and automated grading eliminates need for graders, freeing graduate students for instructor roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recommending or adopting a blended model, include resource-allocation analysis: initial setup costs, staffing model (undergrad assistants vs graduate graders), and savings from automated grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching strategies for developing formal definition-based reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Three primary pathways for development of formal definition-based reasoning about limits: (1) exploring a range of examples to develop a definition that uniquely describes them, (2) developing 'generic examples' through graphical explorations, and (3) extracting meaning from the formal definition itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these pedagogical pathways when designing instruction aimed at transitioning students from case-based to property-based reasoning; the paper studies how metaphorical instantiation can support this transition.
